source: ACIAR Monograph No. 146a, "ដំណាំសំណែកសៀង" [Soybean Growers Manual], Belfield S., Brown C., Martin M. (eds.), New South Wales Department of Primary Industries / Murdoch University / CARDI / ACIAR, 2012
text:
A dedicated chapter covers rhizobium inoculation — treating seed with a peat- or liquid-based Bradyrhizobium inoculant culture before planting so that effective nitrogen-fixing nodules form reliably, particularly important on land that has not grown soybean before (and so lacks a naturalized soil population of compatible rhizobia).

Practical guidance includes: purchasing fresh, correctly-stored inoculant (peat-based products like the pictured "Nodulaid 100" brand, kept cool and used before expiry); calculating inoculant and sticker/adhesive quantities per kilogram of seed with worked example arithmetic (seed weight per hectare × recommended inoculant rate); applying a sticking agent (e.g. a sugar-water slurry) so the inoculant adheres evenly to seed coats; inoculating seed in shade just before planting (not days in advance, since UV light and heat kill the rhizobia); and never mixing inoculated seed with certain fungicide seed treatments that can kill the rhizobia — the manual specifically discusses compatibility issues between chemical seed treatments and live inoculant.

The manual also profiles a companion-cropping/rhizobium-carrier legume (Glyricidia and Stylosanthes species) grown as green manure/forage that can build up soil rhizobium populations, and notes locally-available commercial inoculant brands for mungbean, soybean, and groundnut sold in Cambodia (pictured with labeled bottles), plus a Suranaree University of Technology-developed inoculant product referenced as a research source for further improved strains.
